description: We just need a graphics designer
summary: Next Frontier Explorer is a mission-design game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players plan a real mission, launch it, fly a Hohmann transfer, land, and drive a rover across terrain built from NASA elevation data. The planner uses the rocket equation and JPL orbital elements, and finds the actual Mars launch windows of 16 November 2026 and 4 January 2029. Seven landing regions (Gale, Jezero, Valles Marineris, Olympus Mons, Shackleton, Tycho, Tranquility Base) are built from 16-bit MOLA and LOLA elevation, and the HUD shows true elevation in metres. Players can also target 50 real exoplanets from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. Every prose fact is a verbatim NASA quote checked against its source page at build time, and anything procedural or game-only is labelled on screen. Built for students and the public, it runs offline on Windows, macOS and Linux and includes a 4-minute demo with a before-and-after quiz, so players learn real orbital mechanics and planetary science by doing rather than reading.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Next Frontier Explorer is a mission-design game. A mission runs in eight stages: (1) Mission planner: pick one of 16 Solar System targets or 50 real exoplanets, then a launcher, stage, lander, power source and instruments within a budget, plus a launch date; the rocket equation checks the design can get there. (2) Launch: fly the ascent through Max Q; too much aerodynamic stress breaks the rocket up. (3) Transfer: cruise a Hohmann transfer and make course corrections. (4) Orbit: gather orbital science; gas giants end with an atmospheric probe. (5) Landing: powered descent onto real terrain under the world's real gravity, with fuel set by the delta-v margin you designed. (6) Power-core mini-game: load the rover's power rods without touching the walls. (7) Surface: drive the rover, visit NASA points of interest and collect samples while the HUD shows true elevation. (8) Debrief: score for success, science, budget and tricks. There is also a guided 4-minute Mars demo with a 3-question quiz before and after, and a 2D rocket-builder mode with a parts shop, predicted apogee and a daily leaderboard. Every mission launches from a labelled concept spaceport in Bahrain built from Landsat 8/9 imagery and SRTM elevation.

HOW IT USES NASA DATA

Gale Crater, Jezero, Valles Marineris, Olympus Mons, Shackleton, Tycho and Tranquility Base are cut as 1024 x 1024 height grids from 16-bit MOLA and LOLA elevation (PDS), in true metres, and cross-checked against Solar System Treks elevation (correlation 0.99 or higher). Colour comes from Treks mosaics; gravity, air density and temperatures from the NSSDC Planetary Fact Sheet; launch windows from JPL Keplerian elements (it finds the real Mars windows of 16 Nov 2026 and 4 Jan 2029); exoplanets from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. Fact cards are verbatim quotes from 45 NASA pages, each verified against its source at build time.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students and the public learn orbital mechanics, mission trade-offs and planetary science by doing them. The game is honest about what is real: procedural terrain, tinted maps, computed values and game numbers are labelled on screen, and an in-game Credits & Sources page lists every dataset. It runs fully offline (even from a USB stick) on Windows, macOS and Linux, so it works in classrooms without reliable internet.

TOOLS

Godot game engine (desktop and web builds), Python for the data pipeline (tools/fetch_data.py downloads, caches, cuts regions, builds normal maps and minimaps, verifies facts and writes data/SOURCES.md and data/provenance.json). Sound and music are synthesised in code. Fonts: Space Grotesk and JetBrains Mono (SIL OFL).

CREATIVITY AND CONSIDERATIONS

It joins the whole mission chain, from design trade-offs to driving on real terrain, in one game, and each world's gravity changes how the rover handles. We chose 16-bit PDS elevation over 8-bit Treks tiles because 8-bit gave Tranquility Base only 16 height levels. We avoided NASA branding, and the game states it is not endorsed by NASA.
